title: The Gland and the Council: Houssay, the Chair Taken Away, and the Institute Built Outside the State
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The French House on the Plata

stops.name: Buenos Aires, birth in a French household
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; English and Spanish Wikipedia agree. The coordinate is the atlas's canonical Buenos Aires pin, inherited byte-identical; no source names the house, the street, or the parish.
stops.campa: A son is born to Albert Houssay and Clara Laffont, French immigrants who have made their life in the city on the Plata. They name him Bernardo Alberto. No source gives the house, the street, or the parish; the record gives only Buenos Aires itself, a river port swollen by two decades of European arrival, French and Italian and Spanish families settling into the same grid of streets his parents have chosen. This one will not leave the city for anything shorter than a prize.
suggested_refs: Argentine civil registry entries for Buenos Aires, April 1887, unconsulted in this pass

stops.name: Colegio Nacional de Buenos Aires, the bachiller at thirteen
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Spanish Wikipedia gives the schooling and the age but no month or day, so the date defaults to the first. The address, Bolivar 263, is the school's own institutional address and is not attested by the biographical source.
stops.campa: He finishes the Colegio Nacional de Buenos Aires in his thirteenth year, several years ahead of the boys he sits with. The school occupies the old Jesuit block at the colonial heart of the city, where the country has trained its lawyers and its presidents for a century. Houssay takes the bachiller and goes straight on to the university, with no year of idleness in between. The record notes his birth and then notes this, and it holds nothing at all about the boy in the thirteen years separating them.
suggested_refs: Enrolment and examination registers of the Colegio Nacional de Buenos Aires, c. 1897-1901
sources: Institutional address of the Colegio Nacional de Buenos Aires

stops.name: Escuela de Farmacia, the pharmacist at seventeen
stops.date_confidence: attested as to years: English Wikipedia gives entry at fourteen in 1901, Spanish Wikipedia gives graduation in 1904 at seventeen. The two editions are consistent but reached from opposite ends. The coordinate is a reconstruction of the historic university precinct near the Manzana de las Luces; no source names the building.
stops.campa: At fourteen the University of Buenos Aires admits him to its School of Pharmacy. He qualifies at seventeen, in 1904, a licensed pharmacist before most of his contemporaries have chosen a faculty. The two Wikipedias reach the same boy from opposite ends, one dating his entry and the other his degree, and neither names the building he walked into. He learns to weigh and to extract, to get an active principle out of an animal tissue and prove that it is there. He will not need a second technique for the fifty years that follow.
suggested_refs: Records of the Facultad de Farmacia y Bioquimica, Universidad de Buenos Aires, 1901-1904

stops.name: Facultad de Ciencias Medicas, the student who is already an assistant
stops.date_confidence: attested for the years 1904-1910 (English Wikipedia); no month or day. The coordinate is the atlas's existing Faculty of Medicine pin, inherited byte-identical from che_guevara.journey.json; the faculty's pre-1911 premises may have differed from the Paraguay Street site.
stops.campa: He enters medicine in 1904 and by his third year is working in the physiology department as a research and teaching assistant, paid to run experiments in a subject he is still being examined in. The department is where he stays. Buenos Aires trains him without sending him abroad, and he never takes the European postdoctoral tour that his generation of Latin American scientists treats as compulsory. Everything he knows he learns here, from teachers whose names the record does not keep as carefully as it keeps his.
suggested_refs: Student and staff registers of the Facultad de Ciencias Medicas, Universidad de Buenos Aires, 1904-1911

stops.name: Facultad de Ciencias Medicas, assistant lecturer before the degree
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1908 (English Wikipedia); no month or day, so the date defaults to the first. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from che_guevara.journey.json.
stops.campa: At twenty-one, still an undergraduate, he is made assistant lecturer in physiology. He is teaching the subject he has not yet been examined in. The Argentine scientific establishment of 1908 is small enough to promote a gifted student rather than queue him, and short of men who can run a dog experiment and then explain what it showed. Houssay will spend the next fifty years enlarging that establishment so it never has to promote anyone that fast again.
suggested_refs: Appointment records of the physiology department, Facultad de Ciencias Medicas, 1908

stops.name: Facultad de Ciencias Medicas, the thesis on the pituitary
stops.date_confidence: contested: English Wikipedia dates the thesis 1911; Spanish Wikipedia frames the degree as taken at twenty-three, which given an April 1887 birth fits late 1910 or 1911. The one-year spread is left open and no month or day is given. The quoted paper title is verbatim from a Wikisource table of contents; the article's full text was not reachable.
stops.campa: He takes the medical degree with honours at twenty-three and publishes a doctoral thesis on the physiological actions of extracts of the pituitary gland. The subject of the first document he signs is the subject of the last: the small gland at the base of the brain, and what it does to the body's handling of sugar. Thirty-six years separate this thesis from Stockholm and in all that time the question does not change. His early papers with Giusti and Maag carry the old orthography of the Buenos Aires learned societies.
stops.quote: Accion de los solutos hipofisiarios i de su principio activo sobre la secrecion lactea
stops.quote_source: Houssay, B. A., Giusti, L., Maag, C., paper title as listed in Anales de la Sociedad Cientifica Argentina, Tomo 75, p. 346 (Wikisource table of contents; old orthography preserved as printed)
suggested_refs: Houssay's 1911 doctoral thesis on pituitary extracts, Universidad de Buenos Aires
Anales de la Sociedad Cientifica Argentina, Tomo 75
sources: Wikisource, Anales de la Sociedad Cientifica Argentina, Tomo 75

stops.name: Facultad de Agronomia y Veterinaria, the chair at twenty-three
stops.date_confidence: contested: Singapore Medical Journal 2016 (PMC4728695), peer-reviewed, and English Wikipedia both date the appointment to 1910, immediately on graduation, and the standard Nobel biography gives the tenure as 1910-1919; Spanish Wikipedia alone dates it 1912. The peer-reviewed source is followed and the dissent is not resolved. The coordinate is the campus's documented address, Av. San Martin 4453.
stops.campa: The university gives him a chair of physiology in its veterinary and agronomy school, out at the western edge of the city where the animals are. He is twenty-three and holds a professorship. He keeps it nine years, running a teaching laboratory on livestock while the medical faculty downtown still treats physiology as a lecture course. On the dogs and the horses of the veterinary school he learns what an entire living animal does with what is put into it. Forty years later that is the knowledge separating his work from the biochemists'.
suggested_refs: Appointment records of the Facultad de Agronomia y Veterinaria, UBA, 1910

stops.name: Hospital Marcelo T. de Alvear, chief of clinic
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1913 (English and Spanish Wikipedia); no month or day. Coordinate corrected from the gathering pass by OSM Nominatim, which places Hospital Alvear on Avenida Warnes in La Paternal, about 1.9 km from the value first recorded. The institution later became a specialist psychiatric hospital, so the site is current rather than confirmed unchanged.
stops.campa: He adds a hospital to the two chairs. As chief of clinical services at the Alvear he sees patients whose bodies are running the experiments he sets up in the laboratory, the diabetics above all, whose sugar will not stay where it belongs. For a decade he holds a teaching post, a veterinary chair, a hospital service and a laboratory bench at once, in a city where a man who can do all four is not replaceable. The ward and the kennel are one investigation conducted at two speeds.
suggested_refs: Clinical service records of the Hospital Marcelo T. de Alvear, Buenos Aires, from 1913

stops.name: Instituto Bacteriologico Nacional, the serum department
stops.date_confidence: attested: English Wikipedia gives 1915, Spanish Wikipedia gives the span 1915-1919; no month or day. Coordinate corrected by OSM Nominatim, which places the Instituto Malbran on Avenida Velez Sarsfield in Barracas, about 1.9 km from the value first recorded.
stops.campa: The state hands him its serums. As chief of experimental pathology at the national public health laboratories, the institute that will later carry Malbran's name, he spends four years producing antivenoms and antitoxins for a country with more snakes than physicians. It is the first time an Argentine government pays him to do science rather than to teach it, and the first time he sees from the inside how thinly the state funds the thing it is asking for. He is assembling the argument he will make for the next forty years.
suggested_refs: Serum and experimental pathology records of the Instituto Bacteriologico Nacional, 1915-1919

stops.name: Facultad de Medicina, the chair and the Instituto de Fisiologia
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1919 (English and Spanish Wikipedia), with the directorship running to 1943; no month or day. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from che_guevara.journey.json.
stops.campa: At thirty-two he takes the chair of physiology at the medical faculty and founds an institute inside it. He directs it for twenty-four years and turns it into the first laboratory in Latin America that European and North American physiologists cite as a matter of course. Students arrive from Chile, Uruguay, Brazil, Mexico. In the same city and the same decade Victoria Ocampo is assembling Sur out of another set of foreign correspondences. The two projects never touch. Both are bets that Buenos Aires can be a city other people write to rather than only from.
suggested_refs: Foundation records of the Instituto de Fisiologia, Facultad de Medicina, UBA, 1919

stops.name: Asociacion Medica Argentina, the Sociedad Argentina de Biologia founded
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1920 (Spanish Wikipedia), which also names the premises, the Asociacion Medica Argentina; the gathering pass had wrongly recorded those premises as a gap. No coordinate for the building was verified in this pass, so the stop sits on the atlas's canonical Buenos Aires pin.
stops.campa: In the rooms of the Asociacion Medica Argentina he and his colleagues found the Sociedad Argentina de Biologia, a society with a journal, a meeting calendar, and a standard of proof. It exists to make Argentine experimental biology into a community that criticises itself, rather than a scatter of men each publishing alone in whatever European review will take him. Houssay is thirty-three. It is the first institution he builds that is not a laboratory, and he keeps building them: a continental journal in 1950, a national research council in 1958.
suggested_refs: Founding minutes of the Sociedad Argentina de Biologia, Asociacion Medica Argentina, 1920

stops.name: Buenos Aires, marriage to Maria Angelica Catan
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year and the person (Spanish Wikipedia); no month, day, church, or registry office is named anywhere read. The venue is a genuine gap and the stop sits on the canonical city pin.
stops.campa: He marries Maria Angelica Catan, a chemist and a former student of his, in the year he founds the society. She works beside him for decades. The sources that record her name record almost nothing else: no month, no day, no church, no registry, no account of whatever laboratory work she did in all that time. The chronology of a scientific marriage in Buenos Aires in 1920 preserves the husband's career entire and lets the wife's pass into a single clause. The absence is in the record, not in the marriage.
suggested_refs: Buenos Aires civil marriage registers, 1920

stops.name: National Academy of Sciences, Washington, elected in absentia
stops.date_confidence: the election is attested for 1940 (English Wikipedia); no month or day. No source places Houssay physically in Washington, so the coordinate marks the electing body and not a documented visit.
stops.campa: Washington elects him. He does not go. The National Academy of Sciences takes in a physiologist who has never held a post outside Buenos Aires, on the strength of papers about what happens to a dog's blood sugar when its pituitary is taken out. Election to a foreign academy is a letter and not a journey; it is recorded here because the recognition travels even when the man does not. In 1940 Europe is closing, and North America has begun looking south for science it can no longer get from Berlin or Paris.
suggested_refs: National Academy of Sciences membership records, 1940

stops.name: American Academy of Arts and Sciences, Cambridge, an honorary membership
stops.date_confidence: the election is attested for 1941 (English Wikipedia); travel is unattested and no month or day is given. City and coordinate corrected: the Academy stands at 136 Irving Street, Cambridge, Massachusetts, not Boston, and the gathering pass's value fell about 1.1 km away, near Harvard Yard.
stops.campa: The American Academy of Arts and Sciences names him an international honorary member. Again there is no crossing, only a name entered on a roll in Massachusetts and a notification arriving on the Plata. The gathering record for this journey put the Academy in Boston. It stands in Cambridge, on Irving Street, and the coordinate first written down landed in Harvard Yard instead. The elections of 1940 and 1941 are the sound of a reputation arriving somewhere its owner has never been.
suggested_refs: American Academy of Arts and Sciences membership rolls, 1941

stops.name: The Royal Society, London, a foreign member in wartime
stops.date_confidence: attested (English Wikipedia, cross-checked against the Wikipedia list of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 1943, where Houssay appears as one of only two foreign members); no month or day. His absence from London is inference from wartime conditions and is not stated by any source.
stops.campa: In the middle of the war the Royal Society elects him a foreign member, one of only two that year; the other is Victor Moritz Goldschmidt, a geochemist lately escaped from Norway. The notice reaches Argentina by cable and post across an ocean full of submarines. Houssay does not sail. London, with its laboratories evacuated and its instrument makers turned over to radar, reaches out to a laboratory in South America because that is where the pituitary work is being done.
suggested_refs: Royal Society election certificates, foreign members, 1943
sources: Wikipedia, 'List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 1943'

stops.name: American Philosophical Society, Philadelphia, an international member
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: carried by English Wikipedia alone and not independently confirmed in this pass; no month or day, and travel is unattested.
stops.campa: Philosophical Hall in Philadelphia, Franklin's society, adds him to its international members. One source carries the claim and no other confirms it, and it is marked here as anything standing on one leg is marked. By now the pattern is fixed. While Buenos Aires strips him of his posts, the northern academies compete to put his name on their rolls, and he is more securely a member of institutions he has never entered than of the university that has employed him since he was twenty-one.
suggested_refs: American Philosophical Society membership records, 1944

segments.name: Dismissed, and the Institute Built Against the State

stops.name: Instituto de Fisiologia, the dismissal
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1943 (English and Spanish Wikipedia); no month or day. Spanish Wikipedia specifies that the dismissal followed his signature on a pro-democracy petition, English Wikipedia gives only the political stance; the petition's text and its other signatories were not reachable in this pass. Coordinate inherited from che_guevara.journey.json.
stops.campa: The military government takes his chair. He has signed a petition for democracy and constitutional rule, and the men who took Buenos Aires that year do not want a laureate-in-waiting teaching their medical students. Twenty-four years of the Instituto de Fisiologia end in a letter. He is fifty-six. He does not emigrate, though any academy in the northern hemisphere would have him; he does not appeal. He walks out of the building and starts looking for rooms.
suggested_refs: The 1943 pro-democracy petition and its signatories, text not located

stops.name: Instituto de Biologia y Medicina Experimental, founded in Belgrano
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (ibyme.org.ar and Spanish Wikipedia); the gathering pass had wrongly folded this founding into the 1943 dismissal entry. Coordinate contested: this research pass produced three different values for one building (-34.5556/-58.4472, -34.5548/-58.4457, and OSM Nominatim's -34.5579/-58.4588). Nominatim is used as the only geocoder-traceable one.
stops.campa: Nine months after his dismissal he founds an institute the state cannot dismiss him from. IBYME opens in Belgrano with Eduardo Braun Menendez, Oscar Orias, Juan T. Lewis and Virgilio Foglia, privately funded and deliberately built outside government reach, its running costs met in part by the Rockefeller Foundation. Two years earlier the same foundation had paid for Claude Levi-Strauss's Ecole libre in New York, another laboratory for the politically unhoused. Houssay takes his students with him and resumes the day the rooms are ready.
suggested_refs: IBYME foundation act, 14 March 1944
Rockefeller Foundation grant records for Argentina, 1944 onward
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Instituto de Biologia y Medicina Experimental'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Fisiologia humana
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1945 as the first edition (Spanish Wikipedia); no month or day. The gathering pass dated the treatise 1950, which belongs instead to the run of successive editions with Braun-Menendez and Covian. The source asserts wide translation in general terms and enumerates neither languages nor foreign editions.
stops.campa: Barred from the lecture hall, he writes the lecture. Fisiologia humana appears in 1945 and becomes the book from which physicians are taught across the Spanish-speaking world and, in translation, well beyond it; the editions produced with Braun-Menendez and Covian run on for decades afterward. The government has taken his chair and cannot take his syllabus. Removing him from one lecture hall has put him into every lecture hall in the language, at no cost to itself and against its own intention.
suggested_refs: Fisiologia humana, first edition, Buenos Aires 1945, and its successive editions with Braun-Menendez and Covian

stops.name: Karolinska Institutet, the announcement
stops.date_confidence: the award is attested (English and Spanish Wikipedia); the announcement month is the Nobel Assembly's customary October and the day is not documented here, so it defaults to the first.
stops.campa: The Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska names him co-laureate in physiology or medicine, sharing the year with Carl and Gerty Cori, for the discovery of the part played by the hormones of the anterior pituitary lobe in the regulation of glucose metabolism. He is the first Latin American to take a science Nobel. The prize is announced to a man with no university post, working out of a privately funded institute in Belgrano because his own government dismissed him four years earlier.
suggested_refs: Nobel Assembly minutes and citation, Physiology or Medicine 1947

stops.name: Konserthuset, Stockholm, the medal
stops.date_confidence: attested; Nobel ceremonies are always held on 10 December. The coordinate is the atlas's canonical Konserthuset pin, inherited byte-identical from dirac.journey.json, fermi.journey.json, satyendra_nath_bose.journey.json and richard_feynman.journey.json.
stops.campa: He crosses the Atlantic and takes the medal from the king's hand in the concert hall on Hotorget, the tenth of December as always. Dirac stood on this floor in 1933 and Fermi in 1938, the one going home to Cambridge and the other not going home at all; Feynman will stand here in 1965. Houssay is the first to carry the medal south of the equator. The Coris take the other half of the year for the same molecule approached from the chemistry rather than from the gland.
suggested_refs: Nobel Prize award ceremony programme, Stockholm Concert Hall, 10 December 1947

stops.name: Stadshuset, the banquet in the Golden Hall
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Golden Hall of the Stockholm City Hall is the Nobel Banquet's customary venue for the period and Houssay's attendance follows standard laureate protocol, but no source read gives banquet-specific detail for him individually.
stops.campa: The banquet follows in the Golden Hall, under Einar Forseth's mosaic of the Queen of Lake Malaren receiving the East and the West. Sweden in December 1947 is feeding laureates from a continent still on ration books. What Houssay said at that table, whom he sat beside, whether he spoke French or English: the protocol of the evening is documented and the man inside it is not. He is sixty, and this is the furthest from Buenos Aires he is anywhere recorded going.
suggested_refs: Nobel Banquet seating plans and speeches, Stockholm City Hall, 10 December 1947
sources: Standard Nobel Foundation banquet venue and protocol for 1947

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the return of a laureate with no chair
stops.date_confidence: attested that he returned and remained barred from his university post (Spanish Wikipedia); the month is inferred from the December ceremony and the day defaults to the first. The Guevara overlap is inference from two separately attested facts, not a documented meeting.
stops.campa: He comes home with the medal to the situation he left: no chair, no state laboratory, no reinstatement. The government congratulates the nation on the prize and does not return the post. In April of the same year a twenty-year-old asthmatic named Ernesto Guevara had enrolled in medicine at the faculty Houssay was thrown out of, and passed through its physiology course under men Houssay had trained. The two never meet in any record. They share a building, a city, and a year.
suggested_refs: Argentine press coverage of the 1947 Nobel award, December 1947

stops.name: IBYME, the laboratory of the Peron years
stops.date_confidence: attested for the span 1945-1955 (Spanish Wikipedia and the gathering pool); the stop is dated to the start of the span and month and day default to the first. Coordinate as corrected by OSM Nominatim; two other values circulated in this research pass.
stops.campa: For ten years the real laboratory is the private one. He extends the pituitary and diabetes work the Nobel committee has just honoured, and he trains a generation that scatters into physiology departments from Mexico to Montevideo: Eduardo Braun-Menendez, Miguel Rolando Covian, and dozens whose names the general accounts do not keep. Argentina's most decorated scientist runs the country's best laboratory on foreign philanthropy and private subscription, out of a building in Belgrano, for the duration.
suggested_refs: IBYME laboratory notebooks and publication list, 1945-1955

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the medals of a man with no post
stops.date_confidence: composite stop, dated to the earliest attested award. The James Cook Medal (1948) and the Dale Medal of the Society for Endocrinology (1960) are both single-source (English Wikipedia), and neither entry names a place of award or confirms attendance. The Harvard, Cambridge, Oxford and Paris distinctions are attested by the same source without dates. Pinned to the city where he was living.
stops.campa: The medals keep arriving for a man his own state has no office for. The James Cook Medal in 1948; the Dale Medal of the Society for Endocrinology in 1960; distinctions from Harvard, Cambridge, Oxford, Paris and fifteen further universities, undated in the record and mostly uncollected in person. He receives them in Belgrano. Every body abroad with the power to vote him an honour votes him one, and the university he taught in for four decades will not put him back on its payroll.
suggested_refs: Award citations for the James Cook Medal 1948 and the Dale Medal 1960

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Acta Physiologica Latinoamericana
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1950 (Spanish Wikipedia); no month or day, and the journal's editorial address is not named in any source read.
stops.campa: He founds a journal. Acta Physiologica Latinoamericana gives the continent's physiologists somewhere to publish that is not London, Baltimore or Berlin, and that does not require them to translate first and be read second. It is the instinct of the Sociedad Argentina de Biologia thirty years earlier, worked at continental scale: build the institution, and then the science has somewhere to happen. He is sixty-three and has been building these things since he was thirty-three.
suggested_refs: Acta Physiologica Latinoamericana, volume 1 (1950), editorial matter

stops.name: Universidad de Chile, Santiago, the Pan-American circuit
stops.date_confidence: tradition, not verified: Argentine and Chilean institutional histories describe Houssay lecturing and receiving honours at the Universidad de Chile, but no specific visit, lecture title, or date was confirmed against a primary source in this pass. The date shown is the midpoint of the reported span, c. 1940s-1950s, and carries no authority.
stops.campa: Santiago receives him as the continent's physiologist. The regional histories describe lectures, honours and a standing invitation across the Andes, part of a campaign to make Latin American physiology a single community rather than a set of national efforts each looking north for validation. He arrives from a country whose government has no post for him, and Chile gives him a platform at no cost to itself. The Andes are the shortest border he crosses and the one his students cross most often.
suggested_refs: Universidad de Chile senate and faculty records for honorary awards, 1940s-1950s
sources: General accounts of Houssay's Pan-American scientific advocacy, unverified in this pass

stops.name: Universidad de la Republica, Montevideo, across the estuary
stops.date_confidence: tradition, not verified: regional histories of Latin American physiology describe Houssay as a frequent visitor to Montevideo, but the specific occasions and dates could not be pinned to a primary source in this pass. The date shown is the midpoint of the reported span and carries no authority.
stops.campa: Montevideo is a night's crossing of the Plata, and the histories have him making it often. The Uruguayan physiological school grows in the same water as the Argentine one and shares its journals, its methods and, for a time, its refugees. Two capitals face each other across an estuary a hundred kilometres wide, and the science of both is conducted in one language by men who trained in each other's laboratories. Houssay is the hinge that arrangement turns on for thirty years.
suggested_refs: Facultad de Medicina, Universidad de la Republica, Montevideo, visiting lecturer records
sources: General regional histories of Latin American physiology, unverified in this pass

segments.name: The Chair Returned, the Council Founded

stops.name: Facultad de Medicina, reinstated
stops.date_confidence: attested (English and Spanish Wikipedia) that reinstatement followed the fall of Peron in September 1955 and that he held the post until his death; no month or day is given for the reinstatement itself, so the date defaults to the first of the year. Coordinate inherited from che_guevara.journey.json.
stops.campa: Peron falls in September and Houssay goes back into the building. He is sixty-eight and has been out of it for twelve years. He resumes the chair of physiology and the direction of the Instituto de Fisiologia he founded in 1919, and holds both until he dies. The institute he built in exile does not close. From 1955 he runs two laboratories, the university's and the private one. That is the arrangement he had argued for all along, and it arrives by accident: nobody ever agreed to fund it on purpose.
suggested_refs: UBA reinstatement decrees, 1955-1956

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the first president of CONICET
stops.date_confidence: contested: English Wikipedia dates his directorship from 1957, Spanish Wikipedia gives the presidency as 1958-1971. The disagreement is not resolved here; 1958 is used and the dissent recorded. The founding offices' address is not named in any source read, so the stop sits on the canonical city pin. The line from Sarmiento's observatory is an argument about Argentine institutional history, not a claim any source makes.
stops.campa: He becomes the first president of the National Council for Scientific and Technical Research: state money for research, awarded by scientists, with careers and fellowships attached so that a trained physiologist need not choose between his country and his work. Sarmiento had built the Cordoba observatory in 1871 on the same reasoning, that a republic which will not pay for its own knowledge will import its knowledge and its masters together. Houssay holds the post thirteen years, to the day he dies.
suggested_refs: CONICET founding decree and first council minutes, 1957-1958

stops.name: Instituto de Fisiologia, six hundred papers and the students
stops.date_confidence: the output figure of more than six hundred papers and the mentorship of Braun-Menendez and Covian are attested (English Wikipedia) without any dates attached; the stop is placed in the late working years and its date carries no authority. Coordinate inherited from che_guevara.journey.json.
stops.campa: More than six hundred papers stand under his name by the end, and several books besides. The larger output is the men. Braun-Menendez works out the chemistry of hypertension; Covian carries Argentine physiology into Brazil; the rest staff the departments of a continent. An old man in a laboratory coat on Paraguay Street signs off on other people's experiments and keeps the fellowship applications moving through the council he runs. The papers stop in 1971. The men do not.
suggested_refs: Bibliography of Houssay's published papers, compiled by IBYME

stops.name: Buenos Aires, death at eighty-four
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (English and Spanish Wikipedia, independently confirmed by Wikidata Q237160). The coordinate is the canonical city pin; no source names the house or hospital where he died.
stops.campa: He dies in Buenos Aires on the twenty-first of September, eighty-four years old, still president of CONICET and still holding the chair. He was born in this city, schooled in it, trained in it, employed and dismissed and reinstated in it, and he left it only for congresses and for one December in Stockholm. He may be a man who moved less than almost anyone whose life is worth telling: the map of his life is a map of one city's institutions, drawn at street scale.
suggested_refs: Argentine death registry and press obituaries, September 1971

stops.name: Cementerio de la Chacarita, the grave
stops.date_confidence: burial at Chacarita attested (Spanish and English Wikipedia, independently confirmed by Wikidata Q237160); the date of interment as distinct from the date of death is not given anywhere read. Coordinate corrected: this pass produced two conflicting values about 800 m from the cemetery, and Spanish Wikipedia's -34.5908/-58.4597 agrees with OSM Nominatim to within 200 m. The speculative hedge about La Recoleta is dropped.
stops.campa: They bury him in Chacarita, the great democratic cemetery of Buenos Aires, laid out after the yellow fever of 1871 for a city that had run out of ground. Not Recoleta, where the country keeps its generals and its presidents. Which section, which panteon, which number: no source read gives it. The most decorated Argentine scientist of the twentieth century lies somewhere in ninety-five hectares of gridded graves, and the record stops at the cemetery gate.
suggested_refs: Cementerio de la Chacarita burial registers, September 1971

stops.name: IBYME, the institute that outlived him
stops.date_confidence: the institute's survival and its present dual affiliation with the University of Buenos Aires and CONICET are attested (Spanish Wikipedia); the staffing figure of about 384 and the named directorship sit on a page without a clear as-of date and are provisional. The stop is dated to the year after his death and that date carries no authority.
stops.campa: The private institute he founded because the state could not be trusted now runs under joint affiliation with the state university and the state research council he himself created. Some three hundred and eighty people work there, across endocrinology, neuroscience, biotechnology, oncology and immunology. The building in Belgrano that was a refuge from a government has become a node of one. The refuge and the thing it took refuge from now share a letterhead, and nobody working there has to decide which of those two facts is the point.

stops.name: Argentina, the tenth of April
stops.date_confidence: the national observance of 10 April as the Dia del Investigador Cientifico is attested (English Wikipedia) without a founding year; the stop is dated to the first such date after his death and that year is not attested. Two distinct awards also carry his name and the gathering pass conflated them: an OAS prize dated 1972 by English Wikipedia alone and unconfirmed here, and the Argentine national prize created by Law 25467 article 25 in 2001 and first awarded in 2003.
stops.campa: His birthday becomes the Day of the Scientific Researcher, observed nationally. A country that dismissed him from his chair in 1943 and did not restore it after Stockholm now marks his date of birth in its official calendar. Prizes take his name too, one from the Organization of American States and one created by Argentine statute and handed over by the president. The honour is real and it is also the cheapest instrument a state has, because a day costs nothing and the argument Houssay made was about budgets.

stops.name: Hospital Bernardo Houssay, Florida, Vicente Lopez
stops.date_confidence: the existence of hospitals bearing his name in Florida (partido de Vicente Lopez) and in Mar del Plata is attested (English Wikipedia) without dates, so the stop's date carries no authority. The coordinate and the street address, 1757 Presidente Hipolito Yrigoyen, come from OSM Nominatim and correct the gathering pass's value by about 1 km; the Mar del Plata hospital is attested by city only.
stops.campa: A municipal hospital in Florida, in the partido of Vicente Lopez just north of the capital, carries his name, and another does in Mar del Plata down the coast. The wards carry the name of a man who spent his working life insisting that a country which only treats disease and never studies it will go on treating the same diseases forever. The naming is the ordinary Argentine way of honouring a scientist: put his name on a building people go to when they are ill.

stops.name: Plaza Houssay, the square and the stolen bust
stops.date_confidence: the plaza's opening is attested to the day (Spanish Wikipedia, 'Plaza Houssay'); the theft of the bust is attested only to the decade, the 1990s, and whether it was ever replaced is not stated in the source.
stops.campa: Nine years after his death the city opens a square in his name on the old grounds of the Hospital de Clinicas, between Recoleta and Balvanera, a block from the medical faculty. The chapel of San Lucas is left standing at its centre. A bronze bust of Houssay is set up there, and sometime in the 1990s somebody steals it. The square that commemorates the man who argued Argentina must pay for its own science loses his head to the scrap value of the metal.

stops.name: Neuquen, the dinosaur named for him
stops.date_confidence: the description of Yeneen houssayi is attested for 2026 (Filippi, Bellardini, Carballido, Mendez and Garrido) as is the etymology honouring Houssay, but the month and day of publication were not established, so the date defaults to the first. The coordinate is the provincial capital of Neuquen standing in for the La Invernada locality in the Bajo de la Carpa Formation, whose coordinates this pass did not establish. GBIF returns no hits because the backbone taxonomy has not ingested a 2026 taxon.
stops.campa: Fifty-five years after his death, palaeontologists working the Bajo de la Carpa Formation in North Patagonia name a titanosaur for him. Yeneen houssayi, described in 2026, honours a Nobel laureate in physiology or medicine explicitly for his part in promoting the creation of CONICET, and the men who name it are CONICET researchers. The council he founded to keep Argentine scientists in Argentina puts his name on a sauropod dug out of Argentine rock by Argentines it paid for.
